title: Same letters?
model_restatement: Say True if the two words use exactly the same letters, the same number of times.

clarify.question: Could the words be different lengths?
clarify.answer: They could — then they can't be anagrams.

clarify_fallback: Good question — assume the simple case.
blueprint: Take both words. Tally how many of each letter the first word has, then do the same for the second. Print whether the two tallies match.
draft_code:
a, b = pair
same = set(a) == set(b)
print(same)

checkpoints.prompt: With the fix — after line 2, what is same?

why_line: set('aab') and set('abb') are both {'a', 'b'} — a set keeps which letters, not how many, so the counts difference vanishes.

explain.rule: A set is a guest list with no headcount — 'aab' and 'abb' both invite a and b, so they look like the same party.
explain.bridge: So what keeps every letter, repeats and all, so you can compare them?

fix.rule: sorted(word) keeps every letter in order — two anagrams sort into the identical list.

walk.gloss: Sort each word's letters, repeats kept, and compare.

fix.recommended:
a, b = pair
same = sorted(a) == sorted(b)
print(same)

alternatives.note: Count both words and compare the tallies — the hashmap way.

hints: A set forgets how many of each letter there were.

follow_up.recommended:
a, b = pair
same = sorted(a) == sorted(b)
print(same)
follow_up.fix_hint: Nothing to change — sorted catches the extra a vs the extra b.

one_liner: Same letters isn't the same word — the COUNTS have to match too.

choices.label: True or False: is one word the other with its letters rearranged

questions.prompt: With THIS pair, is one word the other rearranged? Work it out by hand.
'aab' and 'abb' both use only a and b. Is that enough to be the same letters rearranged?

choices.label: Yes — they use the same letters
No — aab has two a's and abb has two b's; how many of each must match too

hints: Rearranged means the same letters, each the same number of times — so tally each word.
Loop over a adding one to ca[ch] (start from 0 with ca.get(ch, 0)); do the same for b into cb. Then compare ca and cb.

why.this_data: Your version is right — it builds two tallies in two loops: 7 lines.
why.real_size: Python can line up both words' letters for you in one line: if they line up identically, every count matches. Let's build that.

blocks.title: Split the pair
blocks.teaches: a, b = pair puts the first word in a and the second in b.

blocks.title: Line the letters up
blocks.teaches: sorted(word) hands back a list of its letters in order — every letter kept, repeats too.

blocks.title: Same list, same order
blocks.teaches: Two lists are == only when they hold the same items in the same order.

blocks.title: A set forgets how many
blocks.teaches: A set keeps each letter once and throws the counts away; sorted keeps every letter, so the counts have to match too.
blocks.code:
a, b = 'aab', 'abb'
print(set(a) == set(b), sorted(a) == sorted(b))

hints: Which line makes a and b exist?
A line can only use a and b after they've been set.
Order: B1's line first, then B4's.
